newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares seen cautious on poor results.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares seen cautious on poor results.

text.p: Indian stocks, dispirited by a string of poor half-year results, are expected to trade in cautious territory next week with negative sentiment putting pressure on prices, traders and analysts said at the weekend.
"The market outlook appears bleak. Stipulations on short selling would have an impact on trading volumes," said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at Lloyds Securities.
"People are likely to adopt a wait-and-watch policy."
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the market regulator, on Thursday announced rules on short selling, requiring brokers to declare short positions on a daily basis.

Stock exchanges have been asked to implement the rule from November 29. SEBI said in a statement all Indian exchanges must ask member brokers to submit their scrip-wise net short sales positions at the end of the day.
"We expect the market to move sideways in the week ahead. In the absence of any market-moving information, trading will be lacklustre," Nucleus Securities said.
The key 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) ended last week 75.16 points, or 2.5 percent, lower than the previous week at 2,890.50, a shade above its three year-low of 2,820.26.
The BSE top-30 share index tumbled 273 points, or about nine percent in November.
Analysts said market sentiment was soured by a flow of disappointing results announced by major companies last week.

India's largest cement firm, Associated Cement Companies, stunned analysts by reporting a 56 percent fall in net profit for the first half of 1996/97 (April-March) to 550.5 million rupees, down from 1.25 billion rupees a year ago.
Other firms which reported lower net profits included Bombay Dyeing, Tata Power and Indian Aluminium.
Traders said the short-term cheer provided by slightly better-than-expected results at market favourite State Bank of India (SBI) would soon fizzle out.
"SBI is the only good hope, but one pillar alone cannot hold up the building," Agarwal said. "By itself, it cannot keep the market sentiment buoyant."
Analysts remain pessimistic, with the latest round of disappointing results adding to the market's worries.

ING Barings said in its latest market report: "The stock market is currently drifting listlessly, searching desperately for direction. We believe the market has yet to complete its downward correction.
"This is born out of the belief that the market has not fully appreciated the grim realities on the political, economic and corporate front," the investment firm said.
"News streaming in from all quarters, whether political or economic, continues to dampen spirits," Nucleus Securities said.
"Only a sustained flow of good information can help free the markets from the clutches of this fierce bear grip."
